title: Carboxylic acids and derivatives
overview: Understand the reactions of acyl chlorides and acyl substitution reactions in more depth. This guide turns the current syllabus outcomes into a connected revision sequence: learn the ideas, practise the method, then use the recall cards and checklist to diagnose what still needs work.
syllabusPoints: Prepare benzoic acid and acyl chlorides and explain carboxylic-acid acidity.
Describe acyl-chloride reactions with water, alcohols, phenol, ammonia and amines.
Draw the addition–elimination mechanism and compare hydrolysis reactivity.

definitions.definition: A reactive carboxylic-acid derivative with functional group –COCl.
Addition to a carbonyl followed by elimination of a leaving group.
A group that pulls electron density and can stabilise nearby negative charge.

sections.title: Carboxylic acids
content: Oxidise an alkylbenzene with a benzylic hydrogen using hot alkaline KMnO₄ then acidify to obtain benzoic acid. Convert RCOOH to RCOCl using PCl₅, PCl₃ with heat or SOCl₂. Methanoic and ethanedioic acids can be further oxidised under the syllabus reagents.
bullets: Write observations/products for oxidising-agent tests where asked.
SOCl₂ gives gaseous by-products that help drive formation.

sections.title: Acidity trends
content: Carboxylic acids are stronger than phenols and alcohols because carboxylate charge is delocalised equally over two oxygen atoms. Electron-withdrawing chlorine substituents stabilise the carboxylate by an inductive effect; more/closer Cl atoms generally increase acidity.
bullets: Compare conjugate bases, not the O–H bond alone.

sections.title: Acyl-chloride reactions
content: At room temperature RCOCl reacts with water→RCOOH, alcohol→ester, phenol→ester, NH₃→primary amide, and primary/secondary amines→substituted amides, releasing HCl. Extra ammonia/amine may neutralise HCl to an ammonium salt.
bullets: Identify the nucleophile and the group replacing Cl.
Phenol acylation does not require the same harsh conditions as direct carboxylic-acid esterification.

sections.title: Addition–elimination mechanism
content: A nucleophile attacks the δ⁺ carbonyl carbon and the C=O π electrons move to oxygen. The tetrahedral intermediate collapses, re-forming C=O and expelling Cl⁻; proton transfer yields the neutral product. Acyl chlorides hydrolyse far more readily than halogenoalkanes or halogenoarenes because the carbonyl activates the acyl carbon and Cl⁻ is a good leaving group.
bullets: Curly arrows must start at electron pairs/bonds.
Show intermediate charge and proton transfer clearly.

diagram.title: Carboxylic acids and derivatives: revision route

examTips: Build reaction maps around RCOCl because one reagent connects acids, esters and amides.
Draw every organic mechanism with charges, lone-pair origin and the leaving group.
Use precise chemical vocabulary, balanced equations and stated conditions; link every observation or trend to particles, bonding or equilibrium.
commonMistakes: Drawing nucleophilic substitution directly at the carbonyl without the tetrahedral intermediate.
Forgetting the HCl/by-product or second ammonia equivalent.
Explaining acid strength without comparing conjugate-base stability.

quickRecall.question: Why are carboxylic acids stronger than phenols?
quickRecall.answer: The carboxylate negative charge is delocalised equally over two oxygen atoms and is more stabilised.

quickRecall.question: What are the two stages of acyl substitution?
quickRecall.answer: Nucleophilic addition to the carbonyl, then elimination of Cl⁻ as C=O reforms.

quickRecall.question: What does an acyl chloride form with a primary amine?
quickRecall.answer: An N-substituted amide, with HCl captured by excess amine where applicable.

quickRecall.question: Why are acyl chlorides highly reactive to water?
quickRecall.answer: The carbonyl carbon is strongly electrophilic and chloride is a good leaving group.
